(p. 79) In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Mumtahanah (The Woman Tested)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, extending to them affection, while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth, expelling the Messenger and yourselves﴾.

He, may He be exalted, forbade the believers from taking the enemy, the polytheist, as allies. The word "ʿaduww" (enemy) is singular, but it is applied to both the individual and the group.

Among its application to the individual is His saying: ﴿So We said, "O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117], meaning by "the enemy" Iblis.

Among its application to the group is His saying: ﴿Then will you take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me while they are enemies to you?﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]. The intended meaning here is the plural, due to the contextual indicators in the passage. Among them is His saying "allies" in the plural; among them is "extending to them affection," which is a plural pronoun; among them is "and they have disbelieved," with the plural waw; among them is "expelling," also in the plural; and His saying after it: ﴿If they overcome you, they will be your enemies and will extend their hands﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 2]. All of these carry plural pronouns.

As for the enemy intended here, he is described in both general and specific terms. He is first described by His saying: ﴿while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth﴾, and he is specified by the description "expelling the Messenger." The description of disbelief includes all of them, so the mention of both together serves emphasis and attention to the specific, like His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. In mentioning the specific here, namely the description of the enemy as one who expels the Messenger and the believers, there is an incitement against those who expelled them from their homes, like His saying: ﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191].

God has clarified who is meant by "those who expelled the Messenger and the believers" in several places. Among them is His saying: ﴿And how many a city, which was greater in strength than your city which has expelled you, have We destroyed﴾ [Muhammad: 13], meaning Makkah. Among them is His saying: ﴿If you do not support him, God has already supported him when those who disbelieved expelled him, the second of two, when they were in the cave﴾ (p. 80) [al-Tawbah: 40], and so on.

Accordingly, the intended meaning of "My enemy and your enemy" here is specifically the polytheists of Makkah.

The commentators have agreed (ijmaʿ, scholarly consensus) that this verse was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, and the story of the letter sent with the camel-rider to the people of Makkah before the conquest, informing them of the Muslims' preparations against them. This supports the intended meaning of "enemy" here. However, although the occasion of revelation (sabab) is definitive in its entry, the generality of the wording is not disregarded. His saying "My enemy and your enemy," and His saying "while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth," includes everyone who disbelieves in what has come to us of the truth, such as the Jews, the Christians, the hypocrites, and whatever new groups have emerged.

The text has also addressed each independent group. In Surat al-Mujadilah, concerning the hypocrites, His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who took as allies a people with whom God is angry? They are neither of you nor of them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 14].

The Shaykh, may God have mercy on him, discussed this.

Concerning the Jews, in Surat "al-Hashr," as already mentioned, and concerning the Jews and Christians together, His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51].

Among the newer groups is everyone who disbelieves in what has come to us of the truth, such as the communists and others, the Hindus, the Buddhists, and others. Among what follows from this generality is what came in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take those who have taken your religion as ridicule and play from among those who were given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers, as allies. And fear God, if you are believers﴾ and ﴿When you call to prayer, they take it as ridicule and play. That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 57–58].

So whoever mocks any part of the religion or takes it as a game and diversion, he is feared to be subject to this verse.

A Note

The mention of the contrast here between ﴿My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ displays the reality of the situation and condemns the act, since enmity is incompatible with alliance and with secretly extending affection to the enemy. Some commentators have debated the question of the order in placing "My enemy" first and joining "your enemy" to it. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi said: the precedence is because the enmity of the servant toward God is without cause, while the enmity of one servant toward another is for a cause, and what is without cause takes precedence over what has a cause.

What appears to be the case, and God knows best, is that the precedence is for a legislative and rhetorical purpose: the enmity of the servant toward God is the root, and it is more ugly, so it is put first. Its ugliness lies in their worshipping other than their Creator, thanking other than their Provider, and denying the messengers of their Lord and harming them.

There came in the sacred hadith (hadith qudsi) what may serve as support for this, in what al-Bayhaqi and al-Hakim related from Muʿadh, and al-Daylami and Ibn ʿAsakir from Abu al-Darda', with its wording: "Indeed I, and the jinn and mankind, are in a great matter: I create and others are worshipped; I provide and others are thanked." And in it: "Their good comes down to the servants, and their evil ascends to Me. I make Myself beloved to them with blessings, and they make themselves hateful to Me with sins."

Likewise, its precedence emphasizes that it is the cause of the enmity between the believers and the disbelievers, and whatever is the cause deserves precedence.

What supports what we have mentioned, that it is the root, is that if the disbelievers believed in God and their enmity toward God ceased, they would become brothers to the believers, and the enmity between them would end. Likewise is the fact that it is restricted by a limit in His saying: ﴿So do not take from them allies until they emigrate in the cause of God﴾ [al-Nisa': 89]. A similar case is His saying concerning the people of Abraham: ﴿And there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever until you believe in God alone﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. So when the polytheists emigrate and the disbelievers believe, the enmity ceases and alliance comes.

From what we have already presented, that the cause of the prohibition against allying with enemies is disbelief, it is known that if there is enmity not due to disbelief, then that alliance is not forbidden, because the fundamental cause is absent, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children there are enemies to you, so beware of them﴾ [al-Taghabun: 14]. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But if you pardon and overlook and forgive, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Taghabun: 14].

So when the fundamental cause of the prohibition against allying with the enemy, which is disbelief, is absent, the exhortation to pardon, overlooking, and forgiveness came, because this enmity is due to another cause, which His saying clarifies: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Taghabun: 15]. Its requirement is only caution lest they tempt him, while the requirement of marriage is good companionship, as is well known. A further clarification of this matter will come at this verse, God willing.

He has explicitly stated the non-prohibition mentioned, regarding those who have not fought you in religion, in His saying: ﴿God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them﴾ (p. 82) [al-Mumtahanah: 8], and the rest of the verse.

Alliance has general and specific rulings. The Shaykh, may God have mercy on him, discussed them in several places in Adwa' al-Bayan:

Among them, in the second volume, at His saying: ﴿And whoever among you allies with them, then he is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], where he discussed it at length.

Among them, in the third volume, presented within His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra': 9], where he explained the bonds of the Islamic world extensively.

Among them, in the fourth volume, at His saying: ﴿Then will you take him and his descendants as allies﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and the rest of the verse.

Among them, in the manuscript of the seventh volume, at His saying: ﴿And how many a city, which was greater in strength than your city which has expelled you—We destroyed them﴾ [Muhammad: 13], where he referred to this verse of "al-Mumtahanah."

Also among them, at His saying: ﴿That is because they said to those who hated what God revealed, "We will obey you in part of the matter"﴾ [Muhammad: 26], where he referred there to earlier places in Surat "al-Shura" and "Bani Isra'il."

Among them, in Surat "al-Mujadilah," at His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who took as allies a people with whom God is angry?﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 14].

What he wrote, may God have mercy on him, contains an explanation of all the aspects of the rulings of this verse. However, I did not find that he addressed, in it, the specific restriction of this verse by His saying: ﴿God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you﴾, and the rest of the verse [al-Mumtahanah: 8].

I did not hear from him, may God have mercy on him, anything about it, although it is an explicit text specifying the generality of this verse. An explanation of that will come at its place, God willing.

A Note

The response of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the orthodox community) to the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), by this verse and its like, regarding their claim that disobedience contradicts faith (p. 83), is that God addressed them with the description of faith together with His saying: ﴿And whoever of you does that has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾. Thus He did not remove them from the generality of their faith by their straying. What supports this is that the straying here is from the "sound way" (sawa' al-sabil), not from the way in absolute terms.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 60, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If they overcome you, they will be your enemies and will extend their hands and tongues against you with evil, and they wish that you would disbelieve.﴾

(Yathqafukum) means: they will reach you (yudrikukum). The root of thaqf is skill in grasping a thing and in doing it, and a thaqqaf spear is one that has been straightened (al-muthaqqaf al-muqawwam).

Al-Raghib said: Then it is used figuratively for attaining something (al-idrak), even when there is no skill involved with it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], and He said: ﴿So if you overcome them in war﴾ [al-Anfal: 57]. End of quotation.

These are the texts of the Qur'an showing that thaqf means attaining (al-idrak). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If they overcome you, they will be your enemies﴾, etc., explicitly states that enmity and the extending of hand and tongue with evil will occur after they overcome them, even though hostility had already existed through their expulsion of them from their homes. So this falls under the category of provoking and of intense warning. What comes after the condition is the extending of hands with evil, because they are now unable to reach them due to the emigration. Among the Qur'an's evidences that enmity already existed in fact among a general group other than the believers is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as intimates those other than your own, who will not spare you [any] corruption. They wish you would suffer; hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 118]. His saying "those other than your own" includes the polytheists, the hypocrites, and the People of the Book. His saying "they wish you would suffer" means in the present. His saying "hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater" is not dependent on the condition mentioned in "if they overcome you." Thus they are enemies, and hatred has appeared from them in word and deed.

On this basis, the verse is a declaration of disassociation between the believers and those other than them. His saying "and they wish that you would disbelieve" has been explained by Allah, exalted is He, as to its cause, namely envy, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back to disbelief after your belief, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109].

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why should you be two groups concerning the hypocrites, when Allah has returned them [to disbelief] for what they earned?﴾ up to His saying (p-84): ﴿They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾ [al-Nisa': 88-89].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 60, verse 3:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you on the Day of Resurrection; He will separate between you﴾.

The word al-arham (the wombs, i.e. blood relatives) is used in the Qur'an to refer to kinship in general, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]. And His saying, ﴿He will separate between you﴾, means: by the severing of lineages between them, as He explained by His saying: ﴿So when the Horn is blown, there will be no kinship among them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101].

He, may He be exalted, has explained the result of this separation between them on the Day of Resurrection in His saying: ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother﴾, ﴿and his mother and his father﴾, ﴿and his wife and his children﴾, ﴿for every man among them, that Day, will be a matter that preoccupies him﴾ [Abasa: 34-37]. And in His saying elsewhere: ﴿and his wife and his brother﴾, ﴿and his kin who shelters him﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 12]. These verses encompass all relatives and explain the cause of the separation between them and its consequences.

This verse is addressed to the believers concerning their relatives among the polytheists, as in the occasion of revelation regarding the matter of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, when he sent a letter to the people of Makkah shortly before the conquest concerning preparations for them.

The implied meaning of the descriptive phrase at the beginning of the context, ﴿My enemy and your enemy﴾ and ﴿and they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth﴾, indicates by the implication of contrast (mafhum al-mukhalafah) that believing relatives may not be separated from them on the Day of Resurrection.

This implied meaning is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith – We will join them with their descendants, and We will not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾ [al-Tur: 21], and His saying, may He be exalted, in the supplication of the angels who bear the Throne for the believers: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to gardens of perpetual residence which You promised them, and whoever was righteous among their forefathers, their spouses, and their descendants﴾ [Ghafir: 8].

This verse is a clear statement that the bonds of religion are stronger and more binding than the bonds of lineage.

This very meaning was previously discussed by the Shaykh – may Allah have mercy upon him – at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most suitable﴾ [al-Isra': 9]. And the verse that follows is a clear demonstration of the reality of this meaning and its comprehensiveness across all nations.

(p. 85) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿There has certainly been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people: "Indeed, we are free of you and of what you worship besides Allah. We have disbelieved in you, and there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever until you believe in Allah alone," except for the statement of Abraham to his father, "I will surely seek forgiveness for you."﴾

*Al-uswa* (example) is like *al-qudwa*, and it means following another person in the state he is in, whether good or bad. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Certainly there has been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21]. Here too: ﴿There has certainly been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4].

Allah the Exalted has explained this required emulation by His saying: ﴿when they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you and of what you worship besides Allah"﴾, and so on.

The emulation here is in three matters:

First: disassociating from them and from what they worship besides Allah.

Second: disbelieving in them.

Third: displaying enmity and hatred, declaring and manifesting it, forever until the stated limit, namely that they believe in Allah alone. This is an extreme form of severance between them and their people, and in addition to it is the display of enmity and hatred forever. The cause of all this is disbelief; when they believe in Allah alone, all of that between them ceases to exist.

Here there is a question: what is the locus of the example, ﴿Abraham and those with him﴾, as indicated by the conjunction linking the two.

Allah's saying ﴿in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people﴾: the speakers of the statement to their people are Abraham and those with Abraham, and this is the point of emulating them in what they said to their people.

As for Allah's saying ﴿except for the statement of Abraham to his father, "I will surely seek forgiveness for you"﴾, this statement of Abraham is not the locus of emulation. The locus of the required emulation in Abraham, peace be upon him, is what he said to his people as a whole, previously mentioned, and what Allah detailed in another place in His saying: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free of what you worship, except He who originated me, for indeed He will guide me"﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 26–27]. This disassociation he made lasting in his descendants, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He made it a word remaining among his descendants﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 28].

As for Allah's saying ﴿except for the statement of Abraham to his father, "I will surely seek forgiveness for you"﴾, and so on, it does not explain here the reason for this exception: is it specific to Abraham's statement to his father, or why?

Allah has explained it in another place in His saying: ﴿And the request of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to Abraham that he was an enemy to Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing﴾ [at-Tawbah: 114]. That promise was made to him at the beginning of his call, when his father said to him: ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so leave me for a long time.﴾ He said: ﴿Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord. Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me﴾ [Maryam: 46–47]. So he had promised him and fulfilled his covenant. When it became clear to him that he was an enemy to Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Thus the locus of emulation in Abraham is this disassociation from his father, when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to Allah.

There has also come what indicates that this is a general matter and not specific to Abraham, peace be upon him, as in Allah's saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were [close] relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of Hellfire﴾ [at-Tawbah: 113]. In this verse and what precedes it is the strongest evidence that the religion of Islam has no following of one person by another; rather, every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned, no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another, and a human being has nothing except what he strives for.

It is remarkable that positions similar to Abraham's stance toward his father appear among various nations. Among them is the stance of Noah, peace be upon him, toward his son, when he said: ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges﴾ [Hud: 45]. Then when his situation became clear to him through Allah's saying: ﴿O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose work is other than righteous﴾ [Hud: 46], ﴿He said, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You that of which I have no knowledge"﴾ and so on [Hud: 47]. So Noah's stance toward his son was like Abraham's stance toward his father.

Among them: the stance of the wives of Noah and Lot toward their husbands, in Allah's saying: ﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, so the two husbands could not avail them against Allah at all﴾, and so on [at-Tahrim: 10].

Among them: the stance of Pharaoh's wife toward Pharaoh, in Allah's saying: ﴿And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, "My Lord, build for me near You a home in Paradise and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds and save me from the wrongdoing people"﴾ [at-Tahrim: 11]. So the wife disassociated herself from her husband. This emulation fully clarifies the meaning of Allah's saying: ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you; on the Day of Resurrection He will separate between you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 3], that is, neither your fathers nor any of your relatives. And Abraham's saying to his father: ﴿I cannot avail you at all against Allah﴾ (p. 87) is explained by what we have previously mentioned: that there is no following in Islam, that a human being has nothing except what he strives for, and that every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned.

And Allah's saying: ﴿The Day when some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before or had not earned good through its faith﴾ [al-An'am: 158], and His saying: ﴿The Day when no soul will possess anything for another soul, and the command that Day will be entirely with Allah﴾ [al-Infitar: 19].

I heard from the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, a lecture in Kano in Nigeria, in a community where some people attach themselves to certain individuals in their beliefs. He presented this subject and explained that no one can benefit another. It had a tremendous effect on souls. Perhaps Allah will facilitate the printing of it along with the printing of all his lectures during that blessed journey.

**An issue**

Some exegetes made this verse evidence that *shar' man qablana* (the law of those before us) is law for us, based on the emulation of Abraham, peace be upon him, and those with him. The verification of this issue is found in the books of legal theory (*usul al-fiqh*). Although this verse indicates in general that the law of those before us is law for us, it is not explicit regarding the point of dispute.

The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, divided the ruling on this issue into three categories:

One category is definitely law for us: that which our law has stated to be law for us, such as the verse on stoning, and like this verse regarding enmity and allegiance. And another category is definitely not law for us, such as the prohibition of work on Saturday and the prohibition of certain fats, etc.

The third category is the locus of dispute: what has been mentioned to us in the Qur'an without our being commanded to do it or forbidden from it.

The majority hold that it is law for us because it was mentioned to us, for if it were not law for us, its mention to us would have no benefit. They cited Allah's saying: ﴿He has ordained for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah and that which We revealed to you, and that which We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: that you establish the religion and do not become divided therein﴾ [ash-Shura: 13], and also this verse. Ash-Shafi'i disagrees regarding this category and says: the verse concerns beliefs, not legal rulings (*furu'*). He cites Allah's saying: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. According to this division mentioned, the verse is not explicit regarding the point of dispute, because we were commanded to emulate him in a specific matter which, in our law, was commanded at the beginning of the surah.

**A notice**

It appears to me in this issue, and Allah the Exalted knows best, that the disagreement between ash-Shafi'i and the majority is almost merely formal, and each is refuted by what the other has argued. It is as follows:

First: Allah's saying ﴿For each of you We have made a law (*shir'ah*) and a method (*minhaj*)﴾ indicates the existence of a law and the existence of a method. When we come to the majority's evidence, ﴿He has ordained for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah﴾, we do not find in it mention of the method. We find in the reality of legislation that the method of what has been legislated for us differs from the method of what was legislated for those before us, as in the prescription of fasting. Allah said: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183]. This agrees in the root of the law, but there came what clarifies the difference in method, in Allah's saying: ﴿It has been made lawful for you the night of fasting to go to your wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. The meaning of that is that it had been forbidden, and it was part of the method and law of those before us. So we agreed with them in the law but our method differed from theirs by making lawful what had been unlawful. This binds the majority. Likewise the rest of the pillars of Islam: prayer is legislated for all, as in Allah's saying: ﴿Purify My House for those who circle it, stand in prayer, bow, and prostrate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125],

• and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, that they may establish prayer, so make hearts among the people incline toward them﴾ [Ibrahim: 37],

• and His saying about Jesus: ﴿And He has enjoined upon me prayer and zakat as long as I remain alive﴾ [Maryam: 31],

and other than that.

Regarding pilgrimage: ﴿And for Allah is the pilgrimage to the House as a duty upon the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], and His saying: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot﴾ and so on [al-Hajj: 27]. So all the pillars, which are rulings (*furu'*) and not beliefs, are legislated in all religions for all nations. We share with them in legislation, but were all of them like our method in their times, their quantities, and their modes? We have found the difference in fasting to be clear, and likewise in other matters. Thus the law (*shir'ah*) is general for all, and the method (*minhaj*) is specific, as ash-Shafi'i says. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

[p. 89]

The repetition of this verse emphasizes the meaning of the first verse.

His saying, ﴿for whoever hopes for God and the Last Day﴾, is explained by what came before it: ﴿if you have gone forth striving in My way and seeking My pleasure﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1]. This is because the two phrases are equal in their referent (al-ma-sadaq, the things to which a term applies). Here the wording is changed to indicate generality, so that it becomes a general principle for anyone who hopes for God and the Last Day: that he should take as an example Abraham, peace be upon him, and those who were with him in their earlier stance.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever turns away, then indeed God is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾. Here *tawalli* (turning away) means turning away from the commands of God in general. It may also refer here to the turning of the disbelievers and their allying with them. Indeed God is free of need of them and praiseworthy.

Ibn Abbas said: "He is perfect in His self-sufficiency (ghina)." A similar statement is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they disbelieved and turned away, and God was self-sufficient﴾ [al-Taghabun: 6].

The clarification that God is independent of the obedience of the obedient has come in both general and specific terms. In the specific case of the Hajj He says: ﴿And for God, upon the people is the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to make his way there. And whoever disbelieves, indeed God is free of need of the worlds﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 97].

In the general case He says: ﴿If you disbelieve, you and whoever is on earth entirely, then indeed God is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾ [Ibrahim: 8]. This is because the deeds of servants are for their own benefit, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever strives, he strives only for himself. Indeed God is free of need of the worlds﴾ [al-Ankabut: 6].

As in the *hadith qudsi* (sacred hadith, a saying of the Prophet ﷺ in which God speaks in the first person): "If the first of you and the last of you, and your humans and your jinn, were upon the most God-fearing heart of any man among you, that would not add anything to My dominion."

He, the Exalted, has clarified His absolute self-sufficiency by His saying: ﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Indeed God is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Luqman: 26].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 60, verse 7:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It may be that Allah will bring about affection between you and those among them with whom you have enmity. And Allah is Competent, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

(p-90) Here he does not clarify whether Allah has actually brought about affection between them and those whom they were enemies with and were commanded to shun and not to befriend, from among their relatives, or not. However, "it may be" (ʿasā) from Allah is for emphasis. Its concluding with His saying, ﴿And Allah is Competent﴾, indicates that He will do this for them. There is also evidence that He actually did it, in Surah An-Nasr (Surah 110), when people entered the religion of Allah in multitudes, and Allah granted them Makkah, and they were freed captives (ṭulaqāʾ) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Likewise was the stance of Abu Sufyan and others, and the Year of Delegations to Madinah after the Conquest. And in the conclusion, "that Allah is Competent," there is an indication that the winning over of hearts (taʾlīf al-qulūb) and the affection between them is only from the power of Allah, the Exalted alone, as His saying, the Exalted, demonstrates: ﴿Even if you had spent whatever is on earth entirely﴾ and the verse [al-Anfal: 63].

And because the affection expected through the guidance of the disbelievers, and guidance is a gift from Allah: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

The Qur'an verse. Allah says: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being kind to them and dealing justly with them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.﴾ ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion, expel you from your homes, and help others in your expulsion, from taking them as allies. Whoever takes them as allies, those are the wrongdoers.﴾

Some exegetes (mufassirun) considered the first verse a concession (rukhsah) to the verse at the beginning of the surah. However, these two verses contain two categories of enemies and two kinds of treatment:

The first category: an enemy who has not fought the Muslims over their religion and has not expelled them from their homes. Regarding them, Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being kind to them.﴾

The second category: those who fought the Muslims, expelled them from their homes, and helped others in their expulsion. Regarding them, Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion, expel you from your homes, and help others in your expulsion, from taking them as allies.﴾

Thus they are two different categories and two differing rulings, although both categories remain within the general scope of ﴿My enemy and your enemy﴾ mentioned at the beginning of the surah. Some exegetes considered the first verse a concession after the earlier prohibition, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword or others, as will come.

They considered the second verse a confirmation of the first prohibition. Some exegetes disputed the claim of abrogation regarding the first verse, and they differed about who it was revealed about and what is meant by it. The reality is that the two verses are a division of the general category of enemy mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], along with explaining each category and its ruling, as indications in the first verse support, and indications in these two verses support, as will come, if Allah, exalted is He, wills.

As for the division, it is two categories: a category that is peaceful and has not fought the Muslims or expelled them from their homes (p-91), so Allah has not forbidden the Muslims from being kind to them and dealing justly with them; and a category that is not peaceful, which fights the Muslims, expels them from their homes, and helps in their expulsion, so Allah has forbidden the Muslims from allying with them. There is a difference between permission to show kindness and justice, and the prohibition of alliance and affection. This division is supported by the indications in the first verse, namely the general description of disbelief and the specific description of expelling the Messenger and you.

It is known that the expulsion of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Muslims from their homes was a result of their fighting and harming them. So this category is the one meant by the prohibition of allying with them, because of their hostile stance, since hostility contradicts alliance.

For this reason He followed it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever takes them as allies, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ What wrongdoing is greater than an individual allying with the enemies of his community and the enemies of Allah and His Messenger?

As for the general category, they are those who disbelieved in what truth came to them, but did not oppose the Muslims over their religion, neither by fighting, nor by expulsion, nor by aiding others against them, nor by helping in their expulsion. These, on one hand, are not appropriate objects of alliance because of their disbelief, but nothing prevents showing them kindness and dealing justly with them.

Based on this, the second verse contains no new discussion beyond the discussion earlier at the beginning of the surah. The discussion remains concerning the first verse, from two angles: the first is clarifying who is meant by it, and the second is clarifying its ruling, and whether it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) or abrogated.

The views of the exegetes have differed on both matters. Given the importance of this subject and the community's need for it at all times, and especially in this era because of the strong interweaving of the world's interests, the depth of their interpenetration, the connection of its parts to one another in all fields, and the inability of any state to be separated from another, the importance of addressing this topic increases.

With Allah's help I will present what has been said about it, and then I will put forward what can be derived from the collection of the views of the exegetes and the words of the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him.

The first view: it is abrogated. al-Qurtubi said, citing Abu Zayd: it was in the early period of Islam, at the time of truce (muwada'ah) and abandoning the command to fight, and then it was abrogated. It was said that it was abrogated by the verse: ﴿Kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. This was said by Qatadah.

(p-92) It was also said: it concerned the people of treaty (sulh), and when that ceased, its ruling ceased and its application ended after the conquest of Makkah.

It was also said: it concerns those with a covenant (ahl al-'ahd), until their covenant ends or it is annulled for them, meaning that it was limited to a specific time and tied to a specific people.

It was also said: it concerned the polytheists among women and children who were incapable of fighting.

It was also said: it concerned the weak among the believers who could not emigrate (hijrah) when emigration was obligatory, and they were unable to do so. In all these views, it has been abrogated by the passing of its time and the departure of those it referred to.

The second view: it is muhkam (definitive). This was also said by al-Qurtubi, who transmitted it from the majority of the people of ta'wil (interpretation). He cited among their evidence that it was revealed about the mother of Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with both of them. She came to her while she had not yet embraced Islam, after the Hijrah, bringing gifts for her daughter. Asma' refused to accept them from her or to receive her until she asked permission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He permitted her and ordered her to maintain ties with her. He attributed this to al-Bukhari and Muslim.

Someone else said: al-Bukhari mentioned it in his History, and he cited from al-Mawardi that her arrival was during the time of the truce. It is known that the time of truce belongs to the first category which was said to be abrogated, meaning by its ending. Accordingly, the verse is, among the exegetes, situated between being muhkam and being abrogated.

When we return to the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of the surah and restrict ourselves to the actual circumstance of the occasion, we find that its beginning was revealed after the end of the covenant due to the polytheists breaking it, and when the Muslims were preparing for the conquest of Makkah. As for the coming of Umm Asma', although it was after the truce, it is unclear whether women were included in the covenant or not, since they are not explicitly mentioned.

Accordingly, the story of Umm Asma' indicates neither the absence of abrogation nor its establishment.

When we return to the general wording, we find the verse explicit and inclusive of everyone who did not show hostility toward the Muslims and did not show any harm toward them. It applies more to the disbelievers than to the Muslims, because kindness toward weak Muslims is known by necessity in the Shari'ah. Accordingly, the claim of abrogation requires strong evidence that outweighs the explicitness of this comprehensive text, and the fulfilment of the known conditions of abrogation in the principles of tafsir (usul al-tafsir).

The view of the majority of the people of ta'wil that it is muhkam supports the absence of abrogation. Likewise is the statement of the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except when you fear from them a fear﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28], that this is a concession in a state of fear and weakness, with the condition that the inner heart remains sound. Its implication (p-93) is that it is muhkam and its application remains valid when necessary. Its implication is also that when the believers are in a state of strength and without fear, secure from them, and there is no fighting from them, and they are in a state of full peace, then there is no obstacle to dealing with them with righteousness and justice. This raises the status of Islam and the Muslims. Indeed, there is in it an invitation to Islam through good treatment, winning hearts through kindness to those who are kind to them, and not being hostile toward those who are not hostile toward them. Among the indications for this, from the signs we noted earlier, is what came in the conclusion of this verse with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.﴾ This is an affirmation of what we presented. It also contrasts this with the conclusion of the other verse: ﴿Whoever takes them as allies among you, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ There is in it a contrast between justice and injustice: justice is in kindness, and fairness is toward one who makes peace with you, while injustice is from one who allies with those who fight his people.

Among what negates abrogation is the absence of contradiction between this meaning and the verse of the sword, because the condition for abrogation is contradiction, the impossibility of reconciling the two, and knowledge of the chronology. Here, reconciliation is possible and contradiction is negated. This is because the command to fight does not prevent kindness before it. Just as the Muslims would not surprise a people with fighting until they invited them to Islam, and this is certainly a form of kindness. Also, they accepted the jizyah from the People of the Book and treated the dhimmis with every kindness and justice.

The story of the woman with the two water-skins (al-zaʻinah), in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, is that they did not fight her, capture her, or seize her water. Rather, they brought her with her water to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He took a little from her two water-skins, supplicated over it, and returned it. Then they drew water, and he said to her: "Know that it is Allah who gave us drink, and you have not lost anything from your two water-skins." They honored her, treated her well, gathered food for her, and sent her on her way. She used to mention that, and she would call her people to Islam.

The story of Thumamah: when he was brought as a captive and tied to a pillar of the mosque, and after he had become unable to fight, they did not prevent themselves from showing kindness to him. He was given milk from seven she-camels every day until his captivity was ended, and he embraced Islam willingly. Thus did the words of His saying, exalted is He, state: ﴿And they give food, despite their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾ ﴿Indeed, we feed you only for the sake of Allah﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Insan: 8–9].

It is known that there was no captive in the hands of the Muslims except from among the disbelievers.

In the year nine, which was the year of delegations (sanat al-wufud), delegations came to Madinah, Muslim and non-Muslim alike, and they were received with righteousness and kindness, such as the delegation of Najran and others. Here is the delegation of Tamim who came boasting (p-94) and negotiating about some of their captives. He (ﷺ) permitted them, listened to their boasting, and ordered some Muslims to respond to them. In the end, they embraced Islam, and the Messenger (ﷺ) granted them prizes. This is the strongest proof that there is no abrogation, because a delegation came challenging and boasting, yet they did not fight and did not help in their expulsion from their homes. They came with a matter customary among the Arabs, and he (ﷺ) went along with them in it, after he declared to them that he was not sent to boast, but out of gentleness toward them, kindness to them, and winning their hearts. And so they embraced Islam. This is what all the views we have presented indicate.

The imam of the exegetes, al-Tabari, examined this question from the angles of transmission (naql). Finally he concluded his discussion with these words, which are their text: "The most correct of these views is the view of the one who said that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion﴾ refers to all categories of religious communities and faiths, that you should be kind to them, maintain ties with them, and deal justly with them. Allah, mighty and majestic, generalized with His saying ﴿those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes﴾ all who have that description, and did not particularize it for some over others. There is no meaning to the claim of one who says that this is abrogated, because the kindness of the believers toward the people of war, whether they are related by blood or unrelated and not forbidden or prohibited, is permissible, provided there is no assistance in it to them or to the people of war against the weaknesses of the people of Islam, or a strengthening of them with horses or weapons."

We have already clarified the correctness of what we said regarding that report we mentioned from al-Zubayr, in the story of Asma' and her mother.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾, it means: Indeed, Allah loves the fair-minded who are equitable with people and give them their right and justice from themselves, so they show kindness to one who is kind to them and treat well one who treats them well. Finished from him.

In the Tafsir of the verses of legal rulings (Tafsir Ayat al-Ahkam) by al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, there is an important discussion which we also quote in its text because of its importance:

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 60, verse 8 (part 2 of 2):

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion﴾. He said: It is said, and Allah knows best, that some of the Muslims were affected by their ties with the polytheists. I think this was when the obligation to fight them was revealed, and the bond of loyalty between them was severed, and the verse was revealed: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadilah 58:22]. When they feared that affection would mean giving them wealth, the verse was revealed: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not drive you out of your homes, from being kind to them and dealing justly with them. Indeed, Allah loves those who deal justly﴾. ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion, drive you out of your homes, and help others in driving you out, from taking them as allies. Whoever takes them as allies, it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾.

(p-95) Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Giving wealth, kindness, justice, gentle speech, and correspondence with them were, by the ruling of Allah, not among what they were forbidden, but only taking them as allies was forbidden for those who were forbidden to be allied with, when they also backed others against the Muslims. This is because He permitted kindness to those polytheists who did not back others against them, and dealing justly with them, and did not prohibit that toward those who did not back others against them. Rather, He mentioned those who backed others against them and forbade allying with them, since alliance (al-walayah) is other than kindness and justice. The Prophet ﷺ ransomed some of the captives of Badr, and Abu 'Izzah al-Jumahi was among those he freed, though he was well known for his enmity and for inciting others against him with his person and tongue. After Badr, he also dealt with Thumamah ibn Uthal, who was well known for his enmity; he ordered him killed, then freed him after taking him captive. Thumamah embraced Islam, and he (Thumamah) withheld grain shipments from the people of Makkah. They asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to permit him to sell them grain, and he permitted him, so he sold it to them.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And they give food, despite their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾ [al-Insan 76:8]. The captives are among those who oppose Allah and His Messenger. End of his words.

This view, which Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) approved and al-Shafi'i affirmed, is what the spirit of Islamic legislation (tashri') requires. As for the viewpoint we promised to present, it is that Muslims today have interests that are intertwined with one another and linked to the whole of the world's nations, including polytheists and People of the Book. A nation today cannot live isolated from the international community, because interests are interlaced and interwoven, especially in the economic field, which today is the lifeblood of production, manufacturing, and marketing. On this basis, the verse helps establish the permissibility of dealing with those who are peaceful and exchanging benefit for benefit, following what Ibn Jarir said and al-Shafi'i clarified, and what the Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned concerning the reality of the Muslims' stance today toward Western civilization, in several occasions in his lectures and in Al-Adwa'. The condition that the Shaykh (may Allah Most High have mercy on him) stipulated is the soundness of the inner state, that is, not inclining the heart. Another condition may also be stated: that this interest is absent among the Muslims themselves. That is, the Islamic world should first cooperate among itself, and if it or some of its states are in need of something found among non-Muslims who have not fought them and have not backed an enemy in fighting them, then there is no objection to cooperating with that state in such matters. Among the practical evidence that confirms all of the above is the conduct of the Prophet ﷺ and his successors after him toward the Jews of Khaybar.

There is no doubt that they fall, first, under His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:1], and the prohibition of allying with them is explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. Whoever among you allies with them is one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:51].

Yet when the Prophet ﷺ expelled them from Madinah and then besieged them at Khaybar, and Allah granted him its conquest, and they came under his control, they were no longer in the position of fighters, nor were they backing others in driving the Muslims from their homes. The Messenger ﷺ dealt with them justly. He made an arrangement with them concerning the land and palm groves of Khaybar and let them remain there in exchange for a share of the produce, as laborers working for his account and for the account of the Muslims. He did not make them slaves to be compelled to labor. Their dealings remained just, as is reported in the account of Ibn Rawahah (may Allah be pleased with him) when he went to estimate the produce for them, and they offered him bribes to lighten their burden. He said to them his famous words: "By Allah, you are the most hateful of creation to me, and I have come to you from the most beloved of creation to me. My hatred for you will not drive me to wrong you, nor will my love for Him (the Prophet ﷺ) make me do so. Either you take half of what has been estimated, or you withhold your hands and you keep half of what has been estimated." They said: "By this the heavens and the earth stand," meaning, by justice and equity. They continued in this arrangement until the end of the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, through the caliphate of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and into the early part of Umar's caliphate, until he expelled them from it.

Similarly, those whose hearts were to be reconciled (al-mu'allafah qulubuhum): the Prophet ﷺ gave to them after the conquest, and Abu Bakr gave them, until Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) prevented them.

We have extended the discussion of this issue because of its importance and the pressing need for it today.

In conclusion: what appears most clearly in this matter, and on which no one has claimed abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one), is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness﴾ [Luqman 31:15]. This is good treatment, kindness, and benevolence toward one who strives to make a Muslim associate others with Allah, even though he does not fight the Muslims. So the right of parenthood takes precedence, even with disbelief and striving toward polytheism.

Likewise, at the end of this very surah, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you know them to be believing women, do not return them to the disbelievers. They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:10].

(p-97) Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And give them what they have spent﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:10]. That is: give the polytheist husbands of the emigrant believing women what they spent on their wives after their emigration. After the wife embraced Islam and emigrated, the marriage bond between her and her disbelieving husband was dissolved, she was separated from him by emigration, and he could no longer reach her. Allah commands the Muslims to give their husbands, who are still polytheists, what they paid in dowry at the marriage and the like, while the husbands remain in disbelief and are unable to reclaim their wives. This is not permission to ally with them, since they are disbelievers. This is part of dealing justly, and Allah knows best.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

Surah al-Mumtahanah. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not drive you out of your homes﴾, and so on.

This noble verse indicates that a disbeliever who does not fight a believer over religion and does not drive him out of his home is not forbidden to be treated kindly and dealt with justly. Another verse has come indicating the prohibition of allying with disbelievers and showing them affection in every case, such as His saying: ﴿Whoever among you allies with them is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:51]; and His saying: ﴿Whoever allies with them, it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:9]; and His saying: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, and so on [al-Mujadilah 58:22].

The answer is that whoever holds that this verse has been abrogated, there is no difficulty for him in it. As for the view that it is decisive (muhkamah), the way to reconcile the verses is understood from it: the disbeliever who is not forbidden from being treated kindly and dealt with justly is conditioned on not fighting over religion and not driving the believers from their homes. The disbeliever who is forbidden from that is the one who fights over religion, drives the believers from their homes, and backs an enemy in driving them out. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 60, verse 10 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, when believing women come to you as emigrants, then test them. Allah knows best their faith. Then if you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers. They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for the women. Give the disbelievers what they have spent. And there is no blame upon you in marrying them when you have given them their bridal payments (ujur). And do not hold on to the marriage ties of disbelieving women. Ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent. That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you, and Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾.

Regarding His saying: ﴿When believing women come to you as emigrants, then test them. Allah knows best their faith﴾, He specifically mentioned the testing of emigrant believing women. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to test them when they did not leave out of aversion to a husband, or to escape some cause and the like. This was mentioned by Ibn Kathir and others.

It has also been said that their testing was by the pledge (bay'ah, the oath of allegiance) that comes later: ﴿They shall not associate anything with Allah, nor shall they steal﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 12], and so on. Its implication is that emigrant men are not tested.

In fact, the Prophet (ﷺ) did not test those who emigrated to him. The reason for testing the women and not the men is what this verse points to in His saying: ﴿Then if you know them to be believers﴾. It is as if emigration alone is not sufficient in their case, unlike men. Allah has testified to the truthfulness of the faith of men through emigration in His saying: ﴿[It is] for the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their wealth, seeking bounty from Allah and approval and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful﴾ [al-Hashr: 8]. This is because a man who sets out as an emigrant knows that upon him is the responsibility of jihad and support, so he does not emigrate unless he is sincere in faith, and therefore he does not need testing. The case of the emigrant Umm Qays does not refute this, because that was a peripheral matter, and it does not prevent the essential purpose of emigration mentioned at the beginning of this surah: ﴿If you have gone out to strive in My cause﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], and so on. Women, by contrast, have no obligation of jihad, and emigration does not impose on them any such consequence. So whatever difficulty confronts them in their lives, whether because of a husband or otherwise, they may leave under the name of emigration. Therefore this required (p-98) verifying their emigration by testing them, so that their faith may be known. This meaning is reinforced by His saying: ﴿Allah knows best their faith﴾, while for men it is: ﴿Those are the truthful﴾ [al-Hashr: 8]. Likewise, from another angle: the emigration of believing women involves a right with another party, namely the husband, whose marriage with her is thereby dissolved, and who is compensated for what he spent on her. The dropping of his right in the marriage and the imposition of his right to compensation are legal matters that require proof, unlike the emigration of men. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying: ﴿Then if you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers﴾, it is known that believing emigrant women, after testing and knowing that they are believers, should not be returned to the disbelievers, because they would harm them if they returned to them. So why does the text specify this?

Many exegetes said: this verse specifies what came in the treaty of al-Hudaybiyya (a place near Makkah). In that treaty, whoever came from the disbelievers to the Muslims as a Muslim was to be returned to the polytheists, while whoever came from the Muslims to the polytheists as a disbeliever was not to be returned to the Muslims. Women were then excluded from the treaty and the men were kept in it, by way of specifying a general ruling. The specification of the Sunnah by the Qur'an and of the Qur'an by the Sunnah is well known. Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) explained this in Mudhakkirat al-Usul and mentioned the principle in the verses of Maraqi al-Su'ud, where he says:

"The Book and the Hadith are specified by it, or by the Hadith absolutely, so take heed."

Among the examples he mentioned of the Sunnah being specified by the Book is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is cut off from a living thing is dead," meaning: it is forbidden. The specification of this general statement came in the saying of Allah: ﴿And from their wool and their fur﴾ [al-Nahl: 80], meaning: that is not forbidden.

Among the examples of the Book being specified by the Sunnah is the saying of Allah: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion and blood﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. The specification of this generality came in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Two kinds of carrion and two kinds of blood have been made lawful for us. As for the two kinds of carrion, they are locusts and fish," and the hadith continues. Al-Qurtubi said: Subay'a bint al-Harith al-Aslamiyya came after the writing of the treaty, while the Prophet (ﷺ) was still at al-Hudaybiyya. Her husband, who was a disbeliever, came and said: "O Muhammad, return my wife to me, for you stipulated that. This is the clay of the treaty, it has not yet dried." So Allah revealed this verse. Some exegetes said that it does not specify the treaty, because women did not enter into it from the start; it applied only to men.

(p-99) Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir also mentioned that Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt came fleeing from her husband Amr ibn al-As, and with her were her two brothers, Ammarah and al-Walid. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned her two brothers and kept her. They said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Return her to us, according to the condition." He (ﷺ) said: "The condition was for men, not for women." So Allah revealed this verse. What appears to be the case, and Allah knows best, is that it specifies the treaty of truce (hudnah), and it is one of the best examples of the Sunnah being specified by the Qur'an, as Ibn Kathir said.

It has been narrated that it is a specifier of the treaty from Urwah, al-Dahhak, Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, al-Zuhri, Muqatil ibn Hayyan and al-Suddi.

Two matters mentioned in the verse indicate that it is a specifier:

The first: it established a new ruling concerning them, namely that there is no lawfulness between them and their husbands, so there is no basis for returning them, and the treaty of truce cannot be implemented together with this ruling. So they were excluded from it and the men remained within it.

The second: it gave the husbands the right to compensation for what they spent on them. Had they not been included at first, the demand for compensation would not have been binding. But it became binding, and the reason for its being binding is that they had the power to prevent them from leaving according to the terms of the aforementioned treaty. So when they left without the permission of their husbands, they were like one who breaks the covenant, and the stated compensation became obligatory for them. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying: ﴿Then if you know them to be believers, do not return them to the disbelievers. They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for the women﴾, in it is the prohibition of believing women to disbelievers. The apparent meaning is that the prohibition arises through emigration, not through Islam before it. The majority agreed that if one of the spouses embraces Islam and emigrates, the marriage bond remains until the end of the waiting period ('iddah). If the other party emigrates during it, they remain in their first marriage.

Here is the case of Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with her husband Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi'.

There has been much disagreement about whether her return to him was by the first marriage contract, or whether he (ﷺ) renewed a new contract for her. Among the causes of this widespread disagreement is linking the date of her conversion with the date of his conversion, between which there were six years. This is an error, because before the revelation of this verse there was no prohibition between a Muslim woman and a disbeliever. Its revelation came after al-Hudaybiyya, and her conversion was in the eighth year. So it is interpreted as meaning that her waiting period had not ended. This agrees with what the majority holds. Ibn Kathir reported an opinion that the Muslim woman had the option: if she wished, she could annul her marriage and remarry after the end of her waiting period, and if she wished, she could wait. End of quote.

(p-100) This opinion has merit, because when she embraced Islam he was no longer a suitable match (kafa'ah) for her, and when suitability is lacking the wife is given the option (khiyar), as in the case of Barirah when she was freed and her husband was still a slave. This is not refuted by His saying: ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for the women﴾, because that applies in the state of the husband's disbelief, based on His saying: ﴿So do not return them to the disbelievers﴾. And Allah knows best.

His saying: ﴿Give them what they have spent﴾ indicates that when separation comes about because of the wife, she must return what the husband spent on her. Whether that is the bridal payment or more, Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) discussed it in the section on khul' (divorce initiated by the wife for compensation) in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying: ﴿And do not hold on to the marriage ties of disbelieving women﴾ commanded the believers to release their disbelieving wives from the marriage bond. Umar ibn al-Khattab divorced two wives on that day, and Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah divorced his wife Arwa bint Rabi'ah. The phrase "marriage ties of disbelieving women" (i.e., the bond, 'ismah) is general to every disbelieving woman, and so includes the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), because of their disbelief in ascribing a son to Allah, as Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) verified. But this generality has been specified by the permission to marry the women of the People of the Book in His saying: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], meaning free women. The prohibition between a Muslim man and a polytheist woman remains by the marriage contract in perpetuity.

The implication of the marriage bond does not prevent retaining one's slave-women by right of possession (milk al-yamin). So it is lawful for a Muslim to enjoy a polytheist woman by right of possession. Accordingly, the prohibition of a Muslim woman to a disbeliever is absolute, whether he is a polytheist or a People of the Book, in perpetuity, based on His saying: ﴿They are not lawful for them﴾, meaning in the present, and ﴿nor are they lawful for the women﴾, meaning in the future. Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) has explained in detail the matter of the forbidden women in marriage earlier, at His saying: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women﴾, and so on [al-Nisa': 25].

Note

Here is a question: if disbelief is the cause of dissolving the bond of a disbelieving woman from a Muslim, and of prohibiting a Muslim woman to a disbeliever, then why is a disbelieving woman from the People of the Book lawful to a Muslim, while a Muslim woman is not lawful to a disbelieving man from the People of the Book? The answer comes from two sides:

The first: Islam is supreme and nothing is superior to it, and guardianship (qawamah) in marriage belongs to the husband, definitively safeguarding the male side, even though they are equal in lawfulness by contract, because equality does not cancel distinctions, as in the case of right of possession. (p-101) If a man possesses a woman, it is lawful for him to enjoy her by right of possession, but if a woman possesses a male slave, it is not lawful for her to enjoy him by right of possession. Moreover, the man's guardianship over the woman and over their children, if he is a disbeliever, means that her religion and their children's religion are not secure.

The second side: the comprehensiveness of Islam and the inadequacy of other systems. This has a social consequence that affects the structure of the family and good companionship. When a Muslim marries a woman of the People of the Book, he believes in her Book and her Prophet, so he will be with her on the principle of one who respects her religion, since he believes in it in general, and so there will be room for mutual understanding, and it may happen that she is led to Islam through her own Book. But when a man of the People of the Book marries a Muslim woman, he does not believe in her religion, so she finds no respect from him for her principle and religion, and there is no room for mutual understanding with him on a matter he does not believe in at all. Consequently there is no room for harmony or accord, and then this marriage has no benefit whatsoever, so it was prohibited from the outset.

His saying: ﴿And there is no blame upon you in marrying them when you have given them their bridal payments﴾ means their dowries (sadaq).

By implication, it indicates that marriage without bridal payments involves blame. This implication is supported by a text in His saying: ﴿And a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes to marry her, exclusively for you, not for the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50]. The giving of herself without a dowry is specific to him (ﷺ). His saying: ﴿exclusively for you, not for the believers﴾ does not make it lawful for anyone else (ﷺ). And His saying: ﴿when you have given them their bridal payments﴾ clearly indicates that marriage is not valid except by giving the bridal payments.

However, there is also evidence that a contract is valid without giving the dowry, as in His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women before you have touched them or specified for them a bridal gift. But give them something﴾, and so on [al-Baqarah: 236].

The jurists have stated the ruling concerning the *mufawwada* (a woman whose marriage contract specifies no dower). If the husband has consummated the marriage with her, then she is owed the *mahr al-mithl* (the customary dowry equivalent to women of her standing). That the word *ujur* (compensation) is applied to the dowry in general is shown by His saying, concerning marrying slave women to one who cannot afford free women: ﴿So from what your right hands possess of your believing young women, [marry them]... to the words [marry them] with the permission of their people and give them their due compensation﴾ [An-Nisa: 25]. And in the case of marrying People of the Book: ﴿And [lawful to you are] chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you have given them their due compensation, desiring chastity, not unlawful sexual intercourse﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 5], and His saying to the Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful to you your wives to whom you have given their due compensation﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 50]. By all of this, the argument of those who take the word *ujur* as evidence for *nikah al-mut'ah* (temporary marriage), based on His saying ﴿So for whatever you enjoy [of marriage] from them, give them their due compensation﴾ [An-Nisa: 24], is refuted. The discussion of *mut'ah* was previously presented briefly by the Shaykh (may God have mercy on him) at His saying ﴿So for whatever you enjoy [of marriage] from them﴾.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And they will not disobey you in what is right﴾.

The qualification "in what is right" (al-qayd bil-ma'ruf) here serves to clarify, and it carries no restrictive implication (la mafhum lahu), because everything the Prophet (ﷺ) commands is right (ma'ruf), and in it is their good. The Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) explained this at the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿When He calls you to that which gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal: 24], in dispelling the appearance of contradiction (ihtira') from the verses of the Book. The discussion of it was already given at the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. However, there is in it an alert that whoever holds a position of command after him has no obedience due to him except in what is right, and knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

The commentators hold that this verse at the close of this surah is like the first verse at its beginning, and this is what is called *'awd 'ala bad'* (returning to the beginning).

Abu Hayyan said: When He opened this surah with the prohibition against taking the disbelievers as allies, He concluded it with the like of that, to emphasise abandoning their alliance, and to repel the Muslims from allying with them and extending affection to them.

Ibn Kathir said: Allah, blessed and exalted is He, forbids allying with the disbelievers at the end of this surah, just as He forbade it at its beginning. What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that it was not merely for emphasis on the earlier prohibition, but that it contains a new meaning, for the following reasons:

Firstly: It is explicit regarding a people with whom Allah is angry. Some have taken it to be general, since every disbeliever is one upon whom anger falls, and it is for emphasis. Others have taken it to be specific to the Jews, since this description became a known designation for them. This is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, as Abu Hayyan reported. Among what the Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) stated in the introduction to *Adwa' al-Bayan* is that if the interpretation of a verse is disputed, and the Qur'an's most common usage is in one of the two meanings, that meaning is preferred over the other. This is established here, as al-Hasan said: it became a designation for them. Allah has specified them in His saying: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He was angry, and of whom He made apes and swine﴾ (p-103) [al-Ma'idah: 60], and His saying about them: ﴿So they returned with anger upon anger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90]. Allah also distinguished between them and the Christians in His saying: ﴿not of those who have evoked anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7]. Had it been said that this verse refers to the Jews and the hypocrites, it would not be far-fetched, because Allah explicitly mentioned His anger upon the hypocrites in this specific sense in surah al-Mujadilah, in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who took as allies a people with whom Allah has been angry? They are neither of you nor of them, and they swear by falsehood while they know﴾ 30 [al-Mujadilah: 14]. On this basis, the verse would be specific to the Jews and the hypocrites. The purpose of specifying these two groups and returning to mention them after the earlier general statement about "My enemy and your enemy", as we have already noted, is, and Allah knows best, that when He first forbade allying with the enemies and commanded the severing of ties with blood relatives, He then followed that with what spreads hope, saying: ﴿It may be that Allah will bring about affection between you and those among them with whom you have enmity﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 7]. The enmity referred to remains general in its scope, but the Jews and the hypocrites did not enter into the implication of that "it may be". So He drew attention to them specifically, lest the believers hope for or await anything of that kind, and so He made them despair of allying with them and of affection towards them, just as the Jews and the hypocrites despair of the Hereafter, that is, through lack of faith, which is the bond of the hope mentioned in "it may be". This happened in fact as Allah reported: He placed affection with some of the polytheists, and He did not place it with some of the hypocrites or the Jews. Therefore it establishes a new meaning and is not merely emphasising what preceded. And Allah knows best.
